newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan AIDS expert considered suicide in blood row.
newsitem.headline: Japan AIDS expert considered suicide in blood row.

text.p: A doctor who was once Japan's top AIDS expert revealed at his negligence trial on Monday that he contemplated suicide when he was blamed for a scandal over the use of HIV-tainted blood products on haemophiliacs.

In the first session of his court hearings, Takeshi Abe pleaded not guilty to charges of professional negligence in the death of a young haemophiliac who had contracted AIDS through unheated blood products.
Abe, 80, was arrested in August 1996 when the mother of the haemophiliac filed murder charges against him.
The scandal involved allegations of a government cover-up and unethical links between big business and bureaucrats.
Abe's case is the first of a series of trials relating to deaths in Japan from HIV-contaminated blood products imported from the United States.
Abe was Japan's leading authority on haemophilia and AIDS during the 1980s when many Japanese haemophiliacs were infected with the disease through tainted blood products.

In an opening statement, prosecutors said Abe recommended blood products that had not been heat treated, knowing the products could carry HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus that causes Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
The charges carry a maximum sentence of five years in jail.
Nearly 400 haemophiliacs treated with unheated blood in the 1980s have died of AIDS and AIDS activists say another 2,000 of the 5,000 haemophiliacs in Japan are HIV-infected.
"As a doctor I truly regret this and I offer my heartfelt condolences to the victim but I cannot accept the fact that I am a defendant," Abe said in giving his plea.
"I was arrested at the age of 80 and I thought of committing suicide inside my detention cell. But then I thought I couldn't die before my innocence is proven in court."
Abe, once the vice president of Tokyo's Teikyo University, headed a research team set up by the Health Ministry in 1983 to investigate the source of AIDS infection in Japan.

The prosecution said Abe influenced the team's decision in March 1984 to favour the use of unheated blood products instead of using heated products such as cryoprecipitate. The Health Ministry did not ban the unheated products until December 1985.
Abe claimed he had no choice but to use unheated products in the 1980s because cryoprecipitate was not easily available, and even if used, tended to dangerously clog blood vessels.
"The use of unheated blood products was an accepted thing in the medical world at the time. I did not have any doubts on the matter," Abe said.
Abe told the three-judge court -- Japan does not have a jury system -- that he did not personally diagnose the patient in question and did not order the use of unheated blood.
"I never injected unheated blood products into the patient nor instructed other doctors to do so," Abe said.

His lawyers also denied prosecution charges that Abe recommended use of unheated blood because of donations totalling 84 million yen ($694,000) made by pharmaceutical companies to projects in which he was involved.

Former Health Ministry official Akihito Matsumura and three former presidents of Osaka-based Green Cross Corp., the top supplier of the products, go on trial on Wednesday for their alleged roles in the scandal.
The victim's mother has asked the court, and it agreed, that her son not be named because she says there is "rampant" discrimination in Japan against the families of AIDS sufferers.
